title: Investigating Photosynthesis Core Test
description: Use controlled comparisons, matter models, and rate data to investigate photosynthesis and distinguish oxygen production from net change.

questions.prompt: A green plant makes sugars during photosynthesis. Which pair supplies the matter used in this process?
questions.questionText: A green plant makes sugars during photosynthesis. Which pair supplies the matter used in this process?
options: Light and heat.
Oxygen and light.
Carbon dioxide and water.
Soil minerals and heat.
questions.correctAnswer: Carbon dioxide and water.
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide and water supply matter; light supplies energy.

questions.prompt: Where does the carbon in newly made plant sugar mainly come from?
questions.questionText: Where does the carbon in newly made plant sugar mainly come from?
options: Carbon dioxide taken in from the surroundings.
Sunlight absorbed by the leaf.
Water taken up by roots.
Minerals dissolved in soil.
questions.correctAnswer: Carbon dioxide taken in from the surroundings.
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide supplies carbon atoms; light is not matter.

questions.prompt: Which description correctly connects light and sugar?
questions.questionText: Which description correctly connects light and sugar?
options: Light becomes the carbon atoms in sugar.
Light energy can be transferred into chemical energy stored in sugar.
Sugar contains no stored energy.
Photosynthesis creates energy from nothing.
questions.correctAnswer: Light energy can be transferred into chemical energy stored in sugar.
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis transforms energy rather than creating it.

questions.prompt: A student says a green plant respires only at night. What correction is needed?
questions.questionText: A student says a green plant respires only at night. What correction is needed?
options: Living plant cells respire in light and darkness.
Plant cells never respire.
Respiration occurs only when leaves turn brown.
Light causes respiration to become photosynthesis.
questions.correctAnswer: Living plant cells respire in light and darkness.
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are distinct processes; respiration continues in light.

questions.prompt: An aquatic plant releases bubbles in light. What should a student avoid assuming from bubble count alone?
questions.questionText: An aquatic plant releases bubbles in light. What should a student avoid assuming from bubble count alone?
options: That every bubble has the same volume and the count is an exact oxygen-production rate.
That bubbles are observations worth recording.
That time matters when comparing counts.
That repeated measurements could help.
questions.correctAnswer: That every bubble has the same volume and the count is an exact oxygen-production rate.
questions.explanation: Bubble size and gas exchange affect interpretation; counts are a rough proxy.

questions.prompt: Why might a healthy plant survive a short dark period without making new sugar by photosynthesis?
questions.questionText: Why might a healthy plant survive a short dark period without making new sugar by photosynthesis?
options: Darkness becomes food in its roots.
Respiration stops whenever light is absent.
It can use stored sugars in cellular respiration.
It makes sugar from oxygen alone.
questions.correctAnswer: It can use stored sugars in cellular respiration.
questions.explanation: Stored organic matter can support respiration when photosynthesis is not occurring.

questions.prompt: A plant produces 24 bubbles in four minutes. What average bubble-count rate was observed?
questions.questionText: A plant produces 24 bubbles in four minutes. What average bubble-count rate was observed?
options: 6 bubbles per minute.
24 bubbles per minute.
96 bubbles per minute.
4 bubbles per minute.
questions.correctAnswer: 6 bubbles per minute.
questions.explanation: Divide the count by the elapsed time: 24/4 = 6.

questions.prompt: To test the effect of light level, which design is strongest?
questions.questionText: To test the effect of light level, which design is strongest?
options: Change light, temperature, and plant species together.
Compare matched plants at different light levels while keeping temperature and carbon dioxide availability similar.
Compare one large sunny plant with one small shaded plant without recording size.
Change the counting time whenever bubbles slow down.
questions.correctAnswer: Compare matched plants at different light levels while keeping temperature and carbon dioxide availability similar.
questions.explanation: A fair comparison changes the factor of interest while controlling other relevant factors.

questions.prompt: A model shows carbon dioxide + water --light energy--> sugars + oxygen. What does it represent?
questions.questionText: A model shows carbon dioxide + water --light energy--> sugars + oxygen. What does it represent?
options: Carbon atoms disappear and energy atoms appear.
Oxygen supplies all of the carbon in sugar.
Water turns into minerals before photosynthesis begins.
Matter is rearranged while energy is transferred.
questions.correctAnswer: Matter is rearranged while energy is transferred.
questions.explanation: The model separates matter inputs and outputs from the energy input.

questions.prompt: Two plants have the same bubble count per minute, but one makes much larger bubbles. What follows?
questions.questionText: Two plants have the same bubble count per minute, but one makes much larger bubbles. What follows?
options: Their released gas volumes must be identical.
The plant with smaller bubbles must release more gas.
The gas volumes released may differ despite equal counts.
Neither plant can be photosynthesizing.
questions.correctAnswer: The gas volumes released may differ despite equal counts.
questions.explanation: Counts do not measure volume unless bubble sizes are accounted for.

questions.prompt: In a simplified closed-system model, photosynthesis produces 8 oxygen units while respiration uses 3 in one hour. What is the net oxygen change?
questions.questionText: In a simplified closed-system model, photosynthesis produces 8 oxygen units while respiration uses 3 in one hour. What is the net oxygen change?
options: An increase of 11 units.
A decrease of 3 units.
An increase of 5 units.
An increase of 8 units.
questions.correctAnswer: An increase of 5 units.
questions.explanation: Net change is production minus use: 8 - 3 = 5.

questions.prompt: A teacher keeps one aquatic-plant container in darkness as a comparison. What can this help reveal?
questions.questionText: A teacher keeps one aquatic-plant container in darkness as a comparison. What can this help reveal?
options: The exact photosynthesis rate in all light levels without other measurements.
Whether water molecules contain carbon.
That respiration happens only in darkness.
Oxygen changes when light-driven photosynthesis is absent.
questions.correctAnswer: Oxygen changes when light-driven photosynthesis is absent.
questions.explanation: A dark comparison can help interpret respiration, but extrapolating its rate requires assumptions.

questions.prompt: A leaf takes in less carbon dioxide after many stomata close. Why might photosynthesis slow?
questions.questionText: A leaf takes in less carbon dioxide after many stomata close. Why might photosynthesis slow?
options: Closed stomata directly remove all chlorophyll.
Less of a required matter input may reach photosynthesizing cells.
Carbon dioxide is only a waste product of photosynthesis.
The leaf no longer needs light.
questions.correctAnswer: Less of a required matter input may reach photosynthesizing cells.
questions.explanation: Gas entry can limit photosynthesis even when light is available.

questions.prompt: Equal-sized plants yield 5, 6, and 7 bubbles per minute in dim light and 11, 12, and 13 in brighter light under matched conditions. Which claim fits?
questions.questionText: Equal-sized plants yield 5, 6, and 7 bubbles per minute in dim light and 11, 12, and 13 in brighter light under matched conditions. Which claim fits?
options: Every plant everywhere doubles its photosynthesis in brighter light.
The dim-light plants did not photosynthesize.
Temperature must have caused the difference despite being held similar.
Brighter light was associated with higher counts in these trials.
questions.correctAnswer: Brighter light was associated with higher counts in these trials.
questions.explanation: The repeated groups support a limited treatment comparison, not a universal rule.

questions.prompt: What is the main value of repeating a photosynthesis measurement with several matched plants?
questions.questionText: What is the main value of repeating a photosynthesis measurement with several matched plants?
options: It guarantees every uncontrolled variable disappears.
It makes a comparison group unnecessary.
It proves the hypothesis before the data are collected.
It reveals variation and reduces reliance on one unusual plant.
questions.correctAnswer: It reveals variation and reduces reliance on one unusual plant.
questions.explanation: Replication helps assess consistency; it does not automatically remove bias.

questions.prompt: A plant grows taller in weak light than in moderate light. Does height alone prove faster photosynthesis?
questions.questionText: A plant grows taller in weak light than in moderate light. Does height alone prove faster photosynthesis?
options: No; stem elongation can change without greater sugar production.
Yes; height is always a direct oxygen-production measurement.
Yes; all growth patterns have only one possible cause.
No; plants cannot grow in weak light.
questions.correctAnswer: No; stem elongation can change without greater sugar production.
questions.explanation: Height is an indirect indicator and can reflect responses to light rather than greater production.

questions.prompt: Which revision improves a model that shows sunlight as matter added to a plant's dry mass?
questions.questionText: Which revision improves a model that shows sunlight as matter added to a plant's dry mass?
options: Show light supplying carbon and water supplying energy.
Replace carbon dioxide with oxygen as the only sugar input.
Show carbon dioxide supplying carbon and light supplying energy.
Remove matter inputs because plants make matter from energy.
questions.correctAnswer: Show carbon dioxide supplying carbon and light supplying energy.
questions.explanation: Energy flow and matter flow should be represented separately.

questions.prompt: One trial releases 36 bubbles in six minutes; another releases 28 in four minutes. Which count rate is greater?
questions.questionText: One trial releases 36 bubbles in six minutes; another releases 28 in four minutes. Which count rate is greater?
options: The first, because 36 exceeds 28.
The second, at 7 rather than 6 bubbles per minute.
They are equal because both lasted several minutes.
The second, at 112 bubbles per minute.
questions.correctAnswer: The second, at 7 rather than 6 bubbles per minute.
questions.explanation: Compare count divided by time: 36/6 = 6 and 28/4 = 7.

questions.prompt: Why are mineral nutrients still important even though they are not the main source of sugar's carbon?
questions.questionText: Why are mineral nutrients still important even though they are not the main source of sugar's carbon?
options: They replace all carbon dioxide in photosynthesis.
They supply all plant energy without light.
They support structures and processes needed for healthy growth.
They are the only material in plant dry mass.
questions.correctAnswer: They support structures and processes needed for healthy growth.
questions.explanation: Plants need mineral nutrients, but their role differs from carbon dioxide and light.

questions.prompt: A lamp is moved closer and both water temperature and bubble count rise. What should be checked before attributing the change only to light?
questions.questionText: A lamp is moved closer and both water temperature and bubble count rise. What should be checked before attributing the change only to light?
options: Whether the ruler was labeled in centimeters.
Whether the plant was named before the trial.
Whether temperature also affected the measured rate.
Whether the same notebook page was used.
questions.correctAnswer: Whether temperature also affected the measured rate.
questions.explanation: Lamp heating can confound an intended light-only comparison.

questions.prompt: In matched trials, count rates at low, medium, and high light are 4, 9, and 9 bubbles per minute. Which follow-up is most useful?
questions.questionText: In matched trials, count rates at low, medium, and high light are 4, 9, and 9 bubbles per minute. Which follow-up is most useful?
options: Conclude that light never affects photosynthesis.
Test whether carbon dioxide availability limits the rate at high light while controlling other factors.
Assume the high-light plant stopped respiring.
Discard the medium-light result because rates must always rise.
questions.correctAnswer: Test whether carbon dioxide availability limits the rate at high light while controlling other factors.
questions.explanation: A plateau suggests testing another possible limiting factor; it does not identify that factor by itself.

questions.prompt: A closed system's oxygen stays constant in light. Which explanation is possible?
questions.questionText: A closed system's oxygen stays constant in light. Which explanation is possible?
options: Photosynthesis must be absent.
Oxygen production and oxygen use are balanced.
Respiration must be absent.
Oxygen is never involved in plant processes.
questions.correctAnswer: Oxygen production and oxygen use are balanced.
questions.explanation: Zero net change can hide simultaneous opposing processes.

questions.prompt: A dark trial uses 2 oxygen units per hour. A light trial gains 6 per hour. Assuming equal respiration in both and no other oxygen exchanges, what is estimated photosynthetic production in light?
questions.questionText: A dark trial uses 2 oxygen units per hour. A light trial gains 6 per hour. Assuming equal respiration in both and no other oxygen exchanges, what is estimated photosynthetic production in light?
options: 4 oxygen units per hour.
6 oxygen units per hour.
12 oxygen units per hour.
8 oxygen units per hour.
questions.correctAnswer: 8 oxygen units per hour.
questions.explanation: Net gain = production - use, so production = 6 + 2 = 8 under the stated assumptions.

questions.prompt: Why is the estimate from a dark respiration rate uncertain if the light trial is much warmer?
questions.questionText: Why is the estimate from a dark respiration rate uncertain if the light trial is much warmer?
options: Respiration may differ with temperature, so equal use cannot be assumed.
Oxygen has no mass when warmed.
Photosynthesis always stops in warmer water.
Dark measurements never contain useful information.
questions.correctAnswer: Respiration may differ with temperature, so equal use cannot be assumed.
questions.explanation: An estimate is only as sound as its assumptions and measurement conditions.

questions.prompt: A no-plant water container also changes dissolved oxygen during an experiment. What does this show?
questions.questionText: A no-plant water container also changes dissolved oxygen during an experiment. What does this show?
options: Background exchange or other non-plant effects must be considered.
Every oxygen change in the plant container must be photosynthesis.
Plants cannot produce oxygen.
The comparison should be ignored because it lacks leaves.
questions.correctAnswer: Background exchange or other non-plant effects must be considered.
questions.explanation: Dissolved oxygen can change through exchange with air and other background processes.

questions.prompt: A class claims that adding carbon dioxide always speeds photosynthesis. Which result challenges the word 'always'?
questions.questionText: A class claims that adding carbon dioxide always speeds photosynthesis. Which result challenges the word 'always'?
options: With adequate light, one plant shows an increase.
Two plants receive the same water volume.
The class uses three measuring containers.
With very little light, added carbon dioxide produces no measurable increase.
questions.correctAnswer: With very little light, added carbon dioxide produces no measurable increase.
questions.explanation: Another limiting factor can prevent a response to more carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Two illuminated samples gain 12 oxygen units in two hours. One has 2 g of plant material; the other has 4 g. Which has the larger net gain per gram per hour?
questions.questionText: Two illuminated samples gain 12 oxygen units in two hours. One has 2 g of plant material; the other has 4 g. Which has the larger net gain per gram per hour?
options: The 4 g sample: 6 rather than 3 units per gram per hour.
They are equal because total gains match.
The 2 g sample: 12 rather than 6 units per gram per hour.
The 2 g sample: 3 rather than 1.5 units per gram per hour.
questions.correctAnswer: The 2 g sample: 3 rather than 1.5 units per gram per hour.
questions.explanation: Normalize by both duration and plant mass: 12/(2 x 2) = 3; 12/(4 x 2) = 1.5.

questions.prompt: A plant container loses oxygen slowly in dim light. What can be concluded without assuming photosynthesis is zero?
questions.questionText: A plant container loses oxygen slowly in dim light. What can be concluded without assuming photosynthesis is zero?
options: Photosynthesis cannot happen at any dim light level.
Oxygen use exceeds oxygen production plus any other net inputs.
Every plant cell has died.
The plant has stopped using sugar.
questions.correctAnswer: Oxygen use exceeds oxygen production plus any other net inputs.
questions.explanation: A negative net change does not rule out a smaller simultaneous production rate.

questions.prompt: Which evidence most directly supports the claim that carbon dioxide contributes carbon to new sugar?
questions.questionText: Which evidence most directly supports the claim that carbon dioxide contributes carbon to new sugar?
options: A carbon tracer from supplied carbon dioxide is later detected in newly made sugars.
The plant's pot becomes warmer in sunlight.
Water moves up a colored stem.
The plant's leaves point toward a window.
questions.correctAnswer: A carbon tracer from supplied carbon dioxide is later detected in newly made sugars.
questions.explanation: Tracing atoms links a matter source to a product more directly than appearance or warmth.

questions.prompt: A report combines higher bubble counts, repeated matched trials, and a temperature check. What conclusion is appropriately cautious?
questions.questionText: A report combines higher bubble counts, repeated matched trials, and a temperature check. What conclusion is appropriately cautious?
options: Light is the only factor controlling photosynthesis for every species.
The tested light increase raised the bubble-count proxy under these conditions; an exact oxygen rate needs additional measurements.
The experiment proves respiration stopped in bright light.
Bubble counts equal sugar mass without calibration.
questions.correctAnswer: The tested light increase raised the bubble-count proxy under these conditions; an exact oxygen rate needs additional measurements.
questions.explanation: Conclusions should match the treatment range, controls, and limits of the measurement.
